excerpt: Carpal tunnel can qualify as an occupational disease in Georgia and South Carolina. How to prove it is work-related, and when to report it.
keyTakeaways: Carpal tunnel syndrome qualifies for workers' compensation in both Georgia and South Carolina as an occupational disease. Georgia requires reporting within 30 days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80) and filing within one year (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). South Carolina allows 90 days for reporting (S.C. Code § 42-15-20) and two years for filing (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). Workers' comp is no-fault — pre-existing conditions and employee actions do not bar claims.

faqs.question: Can I get workers' comp for carpal tunnel syndrome?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both Georgia and South Carolina cover carpal tunnel syndrome as an occupational disease under their workers' compensation systems when the condition arises out of and in the course of employment. You must establish a causal connection between your work duties and the development of CTS.

faqs.question: How do I prove my carpal tunnel is work-related?
faqs.answer: You need medical evidence from a doctor linking your CTS to your work duties, documentation of the repetitive hand and wrist movements your job requires, nerve conduction studies confirming the diagnosis, and a timeline showing your symptoms developed during the period of repetitive work.

faqs.question: What is the deadline to report carpal tunnel to my employer?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must report within 30 days under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80, typically starting from when you knew or should have known the condition was work-related. In South Carolina, the reporting deadline is 90 days under S.C. Code § 42-15-20.

faqs.question: What benefits can I receive for work-related carpal tunnel?
faqs.answer: Benefits include full medical treatment (doctor visits, therapy, surgery), temporary total or partial disability wage replacement (typically two-thirds of your average weekly wage), permanent partial disability compensation if you have lasting impairment, and vocational rehabilitation if you cannot return to your former job.

faqs.question: Can my employer deny my carpal tunnel claim because I have a pre-existing condition?
faqs.answer: Having a pre-existing condition does not automatically disqualify your claim. If your work duties aggravated, accelerated, or worsened a pre-existing carpal tunnel condition, you are still entitled to workers' compensation benefits in both Georgia and South Carolina.

faqs.question: How long is recovery from carpal tunnel release surgery?
faqs.answer: Recovery from carpal tunnel surgery typically takes several weeks to several months. Most workers cannot return to full duty for 4-6 weeks after surgery, and those with physically demanding jobs requiring repetitive hand work may need even longer. Workers' compensation covers all medical expenses and provides disability benefits during recovery.
